\articletype{RESEARCH LETTER}

\title{Channel attention in lightweight hyperspectral CNNs: an equivalence-tested comparison}

\author{
\name{Swati Hira\textsuperscript{a}\thanks{CONTACT Swati Hira. Email: shira@iiitn.ac.in}, Devguru Tiwari\textsuperscript{a}, Pratibha Kokardekar\textsuperscript{b} and S.~R. Sathe\textsuperscript{c}}
\affil{\textsuperscript{a}Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Information Technology Nagpur, Nagpur, India; \textsuperscript{b}Ramdeobaba University, Nagpur, India; \textsuperscript{c}Visvesvaraya National Institute of Technology, Nagpur, India}
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Channel-attention blocks are often added to lightweight networks for hyperspectral image classification, with gains reported on random pixel splits. We test whether such gains are real and whether they transfer. Seven channel-modulation blocks (SE, ECA, CBAM, GCT, SRM and two variants of SNSM, a dispersion-aware probe) are compared on one backbone across five scenes, with no test-based model selection, up to fifteen paired seeds, Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests and equivalence tests with a margin of $\pm$\margin\ point of average accuracy (AA). On random 5\% splits, blocks differ only on Indian Pines, where dispersion-based gates exceed the others by \ipRandGainShort\ AA points through two single-pixel classes. This gap vanishes once every class has 15 training pixels, does not reappear under the same scarcity on other scenes, shrinks at a higher learning rate, and is surpassed by a deeper plain CNN. On random splits of WHU-Hi HanChuan all blocks are equivalent. On patch-disjoint splits accuracy falls by \dropRange\ points, no block is consistently best and differences of two points cannot be excluded. Class counts, host network, training setting and evaluation protocol shape reported accuracy more than the attention block.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
Hyperspectral image classification; channel attention; equivalence testing; spatial leakage; few labels
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
Hyperspectral images record hundreds of contiguous bands. This makes pixel-level land-cover classification possible, but when labelled samples are few it exposes classifiers to the Hughes phenomenon \citep{hughes1968mean,bioucas2013analysis}. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that operate on spatial--spectral patches are the usual lightweight choice \citep{li2019overview,audebert2019review,makantasis2015deep,chen2016deep,zhong2018ssrn,roy2020hybridsn}, and transformers add global context at a higher cost \citep{hong2022spectralformer,sun2022ssftt}. Channel attention is a cheap way to make such networks input-dependent: squeeze-and-excitation (SE) predicts one scale per channel from pooled means through fully connected (FC) layers \citep{hu2018squeeze}; ECA replaces the FC layers by a one-dimensional convolution \citep{wang2020eca}; CBAM adds a spatial gate \citep{woo2018cbam}; GCT normalises channel statistics and gates them with $1+\tanh(\cdot)$ \citep{yang2020gct}; and SRM pools channel means and standard deviations \citep{lee2019srm}. Hyperspectral networks have adopted these blocks widely \citep{mei2019attention,haut2019attention,li2020dbda,zhu2021rssan,roy2021a2s2k}.

Most reported gains come from random pixel splits. With patch-based models, training and test patches then overlap, so test accuracy partly measures memorised spatial context \citep{liang2017sampling,nalepa2019validating}. This leakage has been surveyed \citep{feng2023leakage}, disjoint sampling changes the accuracy of deep models \citep{ahmad2024disjoint}, and spatially separated splits lower the overall accuracy of CNNs and transformers on Pavia University by about 40 points \citep{alkhatib2026leakage}. These studies compare whole architectures. They do not test whether the \emph{choice of channel-attention block} matters, and a block that ``brings no significant gain'' is usually reported without showing that its effect is actually small. In computer vision, careful re-evaluations have found that training and scaling choices can outweigh architectural changes \citep{bello2021revisiting}, that many reported improvements shrink under a fair protocol \citep{musgrave2020reality}, and that seed-to-seed variance must be accounted for before ranking methods \citep{bouthillier2021variance}; we apply this kind of check to channel attention in hyperspectral classification.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item a controlled comparison of seven channel-modulation blocks on one backbone, with identical inputs and schedule, no test-based model selection and paired seeds, in which the absence of a gain is tested directly with equivalence tests, on five scenes under seven protocols that vary class counts and spatial overlap, with checks of host depth, learning rate and feature fitting (Sections~\ref{sec:blocks}--\ref{sec:setup});
\item the finding that the blocks are equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ AA point as soon as every class has 15 training pixels and on the largest scene; the one large difference, on random Indian Pines splits, comes from two single-pixel classes, is matched by a deeper plain CNN, depends on the learning rate, does not reappear under the same scarcity on other scenes, and is not consistently present when patches are disjoint (Section~\ref{sec:results});
\item a recommendation for evaluating new blocks: report the training pixels of the smallest classes, use equivalence tests rather than non-significance, and repeat the comparison on patch-disjoint splits.
\end{itemize}

\section{Blocks compared}\label{sec:blocks}
All blocks are inserted in the same backbone. A $3\times3$ convolution maps the $B$ input features to $C=64$ channels (batch normalisation \citep{ioffe2015batch}, ReLU). Two residual blocks \citep{he2016deep} follow, each computing $\mathbf{h}=\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathrm{BN}(\mathrm{Conv}_{3\times3}(\mathbf{x})))$ and $\mathbf{y}=\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathrm{BN}(\mathrm{Conv}_{3\times3}(\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{h})))+\mathbf{x})$, where $\mathcal{M}$ is the block under study ($\mathcal{M}=$ identity for the plain CNN). Global average pooling, dropout (0.4) \citep{srivastava2014dropout} and a linear layer produce the class scores. SE, ECA (kernel 3, the adaptive value for 64 channels) and CBAM (reduction 16, $7\times7$ spatial gate) output a sigmoid scale per channel; GCT uses its $\ell_2$ embedding and an identity start; SRM gates each channel from its mean and standard deviation through a channel-wise FC layer and batch normalisation.

\textbf{SNSM as a probe.} To test which channel statistic matters, we also include spectral-neighbourhood self-modulation (SNSM), a block whose inputs can be switched on and off. For every channel $c$ it computes the spatial mean, the spatial variance and the difference of the neighbouring channels' means, standardises each across channels, and filters the three with two one-dimensional convolutions along the channel axis (8 hidden channels, kernel 3, dilation 2) into a scale $\gamma_c=1+\frac12\tanh(z_{1,c})$ and a shift $\beta_c=z_{2,c}$, so that $\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{h})_c=\gamma_c\mathbf{h}_c+\beta_c$. The second convolution starts at zero, so the block is initially the identity; it adds 130 parameters per block. SNSM ($\gamma$) drops the shift. The block diagram and the code are in the supplement and repository.

\section{Data and protocols}\label{sec:setup}
\textbf{Data.} We use Indian Pines (IP), Pavia University (PU), Kennedy Space Center (KSC), Botswana (BW) and the larger, more recent WHU-Hi HanChuan (WHU) \citep{baumgardner2015indian,gamba2004pavia,gic2020hyperspectral,zhong2020whu} (Table~\ref{tab:data}). Each band is smoothed with a $5\times5$ Wiener filter, principal component analysis (PCA) \citep{jolliffe2016pca}, fitted without labels on all pixels, keeps 30 components, and the db4 wavelet approximation of each component \citep{mallat1989theory} is resized and appended, giving $B=60$ features. Each labelled pixel is represented by its $15\times15\times B$ patch. \emph{Note on KSC:} the distributed file stores small negative values ($-27$ to $-1$) as unsigned 16-bit integers, which read as 65{,}509--65{,}535 and dominate the PCA. \citet{kakde2018svdd} treated them as saturation and set them to zero, while loaders that read the file as unsigned and rescale it globally, such as that of DeepHyperX \citep{audebert2019review}, keep the wrapped values. We read the file as signed integers; read as unsigned, seven of our CNN variants reach only 77--92\% AA on KSC instead of \kscFixedRange\%.

\tbl{Benchmark scenes and the random 5\% splits (seed 42; split sizes are the same for every seed).}

\label{tab:data}

\textbf{Protocols.} \emph{Random 5\%}: for each class, 5\% of the labelled pixels (at least one) train and the rest test, giving \ntrainIP/\ntestIP\ (IP), \ntrainPU/\ntestPU\ (PU), \ntrainKSC/\ntestKSC\ (KSC), \ntrainBW/\ntestBW\ (BW) and \ntrainWHU/\ntestWHU\ (WHU, test set capped at 50{,}000 pixels) pixels; Alfalfa, Grass-pasture-mowed and Oats then have two, one and one training pixels. \emph{Smallest 15} (IP): the same split with only those three classes raised to 15 training pixels. \emph{Random 50/15} (IP): a random split with the class counts of the standard split, 15 training pixels for those three classes and 50 for each other class (\ntrainIPcnt/\ntestIPcnt). \emph{Standard} (IP): the fixed training and test sets distributed with SpectralFormer \citep{hong2022spectralformer} (\ntrainIPstd/\ntestIPstd), whose training pixels come from separate regions but whose test patches still overlap training patches at $15\times15$. \emph{Smallest 1/1/2} (PU, KSC): the random 5\% split with the three smallest classes of each scene reduced to 1, 1 and 2 training pixels, as in IP. \emph{Hardest 1/1/2} (PU, KSC): the same, but for the three classes on which the plain CNN is least accurate under random 5\% splits. \emph{Patch-disjoint} (PU, KSC, WHU): for each class, the 5\% of its pixels nearest a random centre form a compact training cluster, and every test pixel within 14 pixels of any training pixel is discarded, so no test patch overlaps a training patch (Figure~\ref{fig:split}); \djtestPU\ (PU) and \djtestKSC\ (KSC) test pixels remain, and the WHU test set is again capped at 50{,}000 pixels. This rule leaves no test pixels for five IP classes, and the standard PU and Houston splits were no longer available, so these three scenes carry the patch-disjoint evaluation. \emph{Robustness checks}: a deeper, wider host with four residual blocks of 128 channels (IP random 5\%, KSC patch-disjoint); learning rates of $3\times10^{-4}$ and $3\times10^{-3}$ (IP random 5\%); the blocks applied to the raw bands in wavelength order, without PCA (IP, PU, KSC random 5\%); and PCA fitted on the training pixels only (KSC patch-disjoint).

\textbf{Training and statistics.} Every model sees the same features and splits for a given seed. Training uses cross-entropy, AdamW \citep{loshchilov2019decoupled} (learning rate $10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$), step decay (factor 0.5 every 40 epochs), batch size 64 and exactly 100 epochs, without augmentation or early stopping; the final model is evaluated once. All eight backbone variants use 15 seeds (42--56), except on the random 5\% splits of PU, KSC and BW (five seeds), on WHU and with the deeper host (ten seeds), with the learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$ and on raw bands (five seeds); on the standard split the seed changes only the initialisation and batch order. For each of the \nSettings\ settings we compare SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) with the seven other blocks by paired same-seed differences of AA; the supplement repeats every comparison with the plain CNN as the reference, so that no block is privileged. Differences are tested with two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected within each setting. With five seeds the smallest attainable Wilcoxon $p$ is 0.0625, so those settings are descriptive only. Across all \bhTotal\ comparisons, Benjamini--Hochberg control of the false discovery rate at 5\% gives \bhSig\ discoveries, against \holmSig\ with the per-setting Holm correction. Equivalence is tested with paired two one-sided $t$-tests (TOST, $\alpha=0.05$), because the Wilcoxon test gives no interval: a difference is equivalent if its 90\% $t$ interval lies within $\pm$\margin\ AA point. We chose this margin as less than half the median seed-to-seed standard deviation of AA on random IP splits (\seedSdIP\ points), a difference no single run could resolve; the supplement repeats the equivalence tests at $\pm$0.5 and $\pm$2 points. Runs used PyTorch \citep{paszke2019pytorch} on NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPUs, except ten KSC patch-disjoint seeds, which ran on an RTX 3050 laptop GPU for all blocks and are pooled with the five T4 seeds; each paired difference compares blocks run on the same GPU.

\textbf{Random 5\% splits.} On PU, KSC and BW the eight variants lie within \randOtherSpread\ AA points of each other (Table~\ref{tab:main}), and on WHU, the largest scene, within \spreadWHUrand\ points, with every comparison equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ point (Tables~\ref{tab:protocol_dj} and \ref{tab:paired}). On these scenes AA is close to 99\%, and WHU has \ntrainWHU\ training pixels, so this equivalence partly reflects a ceiling and an ample training set; the few-label case is tested on IP and by the scarcity protocols below. Only IP separates them: SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) is significantly better than the plain CNN, SE, ECA, CBAM and GCT, by \ipRandGain\ points, but not than SRM or SNSM ($\gamma$) (Table~\ref{tab:paired}), while the overall accuracy of all eight differs by only \ipRandOAspread\ points. The gap lies almost entirely in the two classes with a single training pixel and 19 and 27 test pixels: SRM and the SNSM variants reach \pcGpmDisp\% on Grass-pasture-mowed and \pcOatsDisp\% on Oats, against \pcGpmRest\% and \pcOatsRest\% for the other blocks, whereas on Alfalfa (two training pixels) all blocks lie within \pcAlfalfaSpread\ points and their mean over the other 13 classes differs by less than one point.

\textbf{Class counts.} Raising only the three smallest IP classes to 15 training pixels shrinks the spread of block means from \spreadIPRand\ to \spreadIPSmall\ points (Table~\ref{tab:protocol_ip}). SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) keeps a small edge of \smallGain\ points over every block, significant per setting but for only \bhSmallKeep\ of the seven blocks under the global correction, and every one of these differences is also equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ point (Table~\ref{tab:paired}). With 15--50 training pixels per class, in the random 50/15 split or the standard split, the block means span \spreadIPCnt\ and \spreadIPStd\ points and all fourteen comparisons are equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ point; only the difference against ECA on the standard split (\stdEcaDiff\ points) is also significant. Because the random 50/15 split keeps the random geometry and changes only the class counts, the IP gap is an effect of the single-pixel classes, not of spatial leakage.

\textbf{Scarcity elsewhere.} Reducing the three smallest classes of PU and KSC to 1, 1 and 2 training pixels lowers AA by about \dropScarcePU\ and \dropScarceKSC\ points, but the dispersion-based gates do not gain (Table~\ref{tab:paired}): on PU, SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) has the lowest mean AA and is significantly worse than ECA and SNSM ($\gamma$); on KSC no difference is significant. Making the three \emph{hardest} classes scarce instead gives the same picture: all differences stay within \hardMax\ points and none is significant. Per-block AA is in the supplement.

\textbf{Patch-disjoint splits.} Removing patch overlap lowers AA by \dropPU\ points on PU, \dropKSC\ on KSC and \dropWHU\ on WHU, averaged over blocks, and OA to \djOAPU\%, \djOAKSC\% and \djOAWHU\% (Table~\ref{tab:protocol_dj}). Block means span \spreadDJPU\ (PU), \spreadDJKSC\ (KSC) and \spreadDJWHU\ (WHU) points, but the seed-to-seed standard deviation is \djStdRange\ points and the median 95\% interval of a paired difference is \ciwPUdj\ (PU) and \ciwKSCdj\ (KSC) points wide, so differences of about two points can be neither confirmed nor excluded: no comparison is equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ point, and at most one per scene within $\pm$2 points. On PU no difference is significant; on KSC, SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) is significantly better than the plain CNN, GCT and SRM (SRM not under the global correction), but not than SE, ECA, CBAM or SNSM ($\gamma$), and SE has the highest mean AA (Figure~\ref{fig:paired}); against the plain CNN, only SE and SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) are significantly better on KSC; on WHU, SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) has the lowest mean AA (\whuDisjAA\% across blocks) and no difference is significant. The ranking also changes between protocols: SRM, tied best on random 5\% IP, is the lowest on patch-disjoint KSC.

\textbf{Host network, learning rate and features.} In the deeper, wider host the Indian Pines block means span only \deepIPspread\ points, SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) is no longer the best block, the plain CNN reaches \deepPlainIP\% AA, more than any block in the shallow host (at most \shallowBestIP\%), and on patch-disjoint KSC no difference is significant (Table~\ref{tab:paired}; per-block AA in the supplement). Fitting PCA on the training pixels only leaves patch-disjoint KSC accuracy unchanged (\trainPcaRange\% against \scenePcaRange\% AA across blocks), so the scene-level PCA does not inflate these results. The learning rate changes the size of the Indian Pines gap. With $3\times10^{-3}$ the plain CNN rises from \plainIP\% to \plainLrHigh\% AA, SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) exceeds the other blocks by at most \lrHighMax\ points and no difference is significant (\nseedsLrHigh\ seeds). With $3\times10^{-4}$ all blocks undertrain in 100 epochs and SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) degrades least, by \lrLowGain\ points over the others (five seeds, descriptive only). The single-pixel-class gap is thus largely a property of the host network and the optimisation setting.

\textbf{Which statistic matters.} Removing inputs from the SNSM probe on random 5\% IP (five seeds, descriptive only; Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) shows that the variance carries the gap: with the mean alone AA falls by \ablMeanDrop\ points, adding the gradient to the mean does not recover it, and mean and variance alone are \ablVarGain\ points better than the full probe (\ablVarWins\ of five seeds), so the gradient input is not needed; without the zero initialisation AA is lower on all five seeds. This matches the tie between SNSM and SRM, the only other block that gates on dispersion. Applied to the raw bands in wavelength order instead of the PCA features (five seeds; repository), the blocks show the same pattern: within \bandOtherSpread\ AA points of each other on PU and KSC, while on IP SNSM ($\gamma{+}\beta$) exceeds the others by \bandIPgain\ points. All blocks add at most a few thousand parameters; SNSM's many small operations make its batch-1 latency about \latencyRatio\ times that of the plain CNN (supplement).

\section{Discussion and limitations}
Across five scenes and seven protocols, the choice of channel-attention block produced a large and consistent difference in one setting only: random 5\% splits of Indian Pines, where two classes have a single training pixel. There, gates that see channel dispersion recognised those classes more often, but the size of the gap depended on the host network and the learning rate. With 15 or more training pixels per class, and on random splits of the large WHU-Hi scene, all blocks were equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ AA point, and making the smallest or the hardest classes of Pavia University and KSC equally scarce did not favour dispersion-based gates. Spatial leakage moved accuracy far more than any block did: without patch overlap every block lost more than 30 AA points, the ranking of the blocks changed, and the remaining differences were mostly not significant, although differences of about two points could not be excluded. A gain reported for a new block on a random split should therefore be checked for its dependence on the smallest classes, tested for equivalence rather than for significance alone, and repeated on patch-disjoint splits.

Several limitations apply. The blocks were compared in two residual hosts of one architecture family, with one patch size and one feature pipeline; transformer hosts may use attention differently. No block was tuned individually: of two other learning rates, the higher one (15 seeds) removed the significant Indian Pines gap and the lower one (five seeds) widened it, so a per-block tuning study could change the size of that single-scene effect. On the patch-disjoint splits, 10--15 seeds can only exclude differences larger than about two points, and the construction adds a spatial shift between training and test data; the standard IP split still lets patches overlap, and the standard PU and Houston splits were unavailable.

\section{Conclusion}
In lightweight hyperspectral CNNs, seven channel-attention blocks were equivalent within $\pm$\margin\ point of average accuracy whenever every class had at least 15 training pixels, and on random splits of the large WHU-Hi scene. The one large difference, \ipRandGainInt\ points in favour of dispersion-based gates on random Indian Pines splits, came from two single-pixel classes. A deeper plain CNN (\deepPlainIP\% AA) exceeded every shallow block (at most \shallowBestIP\%), the gap depended on the learning rate, it did not appear when the same scarcity was imposed on other scenes, and it was mostly not significant on patch-disjoint splits, where accuracy dropped by \dropRange\ points. There no block was consistently best, although differences of about two points could not be excluded. Class counts, host network, training setting and evaluation protocol shaped reported accuracy more than the choice of attention block.
